sentences.text: The red rail possessed reddish hairlike feathers, dark legs, and a long curved beak. It had small wings and slender legs relative to its body size.
This bird measured approximately 35 to 40 cm long, with males weighing around 1.3 kg and females around 1 kg.
Like other birds native to the island, the red rail had lost the ability to fly.
The only unequivocal colored depiction of the red rail shows its plumage as reddish brown.
Fossil snail shells found with damage matching its beak attacks provide evidence of its feeding habits.
The bird could be easily lured by showing it a red cloth, to which it would approach to attack.
Hume suggested that the red rail was able to swallow snails whole.
The red rail was first mentioned in 1598 by Dutch pilot Heyndrick Dircksz Jolinck as "Indian river woodcocks".
The red rail became extinct shortly after 1693.
The last recorded sighting of a red rail was in 1693, with extinction occurring around 1700 due to human predation and introduced species.
François Leguat was the last source to mention the red rail, leading to the assumption that it went extinct in the early 1700s.
A 1660s report by Johannes Pretorius, published in 2015, mentions that the red rail scratched in the earth with sharp claws to find food such as worms under fallen leaves.
Hume suggested that the worms mentioned by Pretorius were likely endemic nemertean and planarian worms found in leaf-litter and rotten wood.
Milne-Edwards suggested that the red rail fed by crushing molluscs and other shells because its bill tip was sharp and strong.
Subfossil shells found with puncture holes suggest predation by birds, likely matching attacks from the red rail's beak.
According to Cheke, the red rail's ground-nesting habit made it vulnerable to introduced animals like pigs that ate its eggs and young, likely contributing to its extinction.
Because the red rail nested on the ground, pigs ate its eggs and chicks, which likely contributed to its extinction.
Hume suggested that the red rail was driven to extinction because it was inquisitive and fearless, making it easy prey for feral cats.
Cheke and Hume suggested in 2008 that the red rail's loss of feather structure indicated long-term isolation.
The red rail belongs to the extinct genus Aphanapteryx.
The red rail is commonly classified in its own genus, Aphanapteryx, but has historically been united with the Rodrigues rail in the genus Erythromachus.
The genus Aphanapteryx belongs to the subfamily Rallinae.
Apterornis bonasia is a synonym of Aphanapteryx bonasia, originally described by Selys in 1848.
Japanese ornithologist Masauji Hachisuka used a 1638 account of yellowish coloration to argue for a distinct species, Kuina mundyi, rather than the red rail.
Henry Ogg Forbes described the extinct Hawkins's rail as a new species of Aphanapteryx in 1892.
The red rail was endemic to Mauritius.
The genus Aphanapteryx lived during the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
Julian Hume suggested the ancestors of the red rail may have arrived on the Mascarenes as early as the middle Miocene, though this might be more recent.
The red rail had a close relative on Rodrigues Island known as the extinct Rodrigues rail, which is sometimes considered to be in the same genus.
Gadow proposed that the similarities between the red rail and the Chatham Islands rail resulted from parallel evolution.
Hume doubted the identification of red rails in paintings by Roelant Savery, suggesting they may instead show Eurasian bitterns.
Hume concluded that paintings by Jan Brueghel the Elder showing a bird resembling a red rail actually depict Eurasian bitterns.
In 2008, Cheke suggested that all references to "dodos" after 1662 actually refer to the red rail.
